service.name: Wedding ceremony music
service.serviceType: Acoustic and Spanish guitar for wedding ceremonies
service.description: An acoustic or Spanish guitarist for a wedding ceremony prelude, processional and recessional, with an announcement microphone for the officiant, across Denver, the Front Range and the Colorado mountain corridor.

faqs.a: In four parts, in this order. A prelude while guests are seated, a processional for the wedding party and the entrance, an optional interlude during a reading or a unity moment, and a recessional on the way back out. The player watches the aisle rather than a clock, and stretches or ends a piece to match what is actually happening.

faqs.q: How many songs for a ceremony?
faqs.a: Three named ones, plus a prelude that runs continuously. The three you choose are the processional, the recessional and, if the ceremony has a still moment in it, one interlude. The prelude is not chosen song by song: it is twenty to thirty minutes of playing while guests arrive and sit down.

faqs.q: How long should ceremony music be?
faqs.a: About 45 to 60 minutes of playing in total. Twenty to thirty minutes of prelude before the start, then the ceremony itself, which usually runs twenty to thirty minutes for a civil or non-denominational service and longer for a religious one. Booking the hour before the ceremony is what stops guests sitting in silence.

For the prelude and the processional, yes. A lyric pulls attention to the words at the moment everyone is watching the aisle, and a vocal competes with the walk instead of carrying it. An interlude is where a sung song works, because the guests are seated and still and there is nothing else to look at.

The music that plays while guests arrive and take their seats, usually twenty to thirty minutes before the ceremony starts. It has no set list and no cue: it runs continuously, at a volume people can greet each other over, and it ends when the officiant is in place. Its job is to make an empty waiting stretch feel hosted.

A solo musician, a small ensemble, or the DJ. In Colorado the common choices are a guitarist, a string duo or trio, a harpist, or the reception DJ running recorded tracks through a second speaker. A guitarist is the most portable of them and the only one that reliably plays outdoors without a stage.

Yes, most will, and it is a reasonable choice when the ceremony and the reception are in the same building. What a DJ brings is a second speaker and a microphone for the officiant. What recorded tracks cannot do is stretch to fit a longer aisle or land the last chord on the kiss, which is the part live players are hired for.

faqs.q: How much to tip ceremony musicians?
faqs.a: Nothing is expected here. A contracted ensemble is booked at a figure agreed for your date and that figure is the whole cost of the music, so a gratuity is a personal choice rather than a convention you are missing. Where it is customary is with an individual performer hired directly and informally. If you want to do something that lands, credit the players by name to your photographer before the gallery is submitted.
